articles.title: Drunk driver jailed after Rochdale police pursuit left pedestrian with life-changing injuries
articles.excerpt: Cameron Grainger fled officers through Rochdale town centre after a night drinking. A man was seriously injured when he was struck by the police car trying to stop him.
articles.content_html:
A man who led police on a pursuit through Rochdale after an evening of drinking has been jailed for more than four years.

Cameron Grainger was found guilty of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court today (Friday 6 November), Greater Manchester Police said. He was also banned from driving for six years and two months.

The court heard that at about 1am on Sunday 19 November 2023, Grainger parked his Seat Leon in the Upper Broadfield car park in Rochdale town centre and spent almost three hours in bars and pubs nearby with three friends.

CCTV operators watching the town centre saw him return to the car at around 3.25am and alerted police that a man who appeared intoxicated was about to drive away. Officers were given a description of the car, its registration and where it was leaving from.

When officers tried to stop the car as it left the town centre, Grainger failed to stop. CCTV showed him driving at speed along Rochdale Road and on the wrong side of the road throughout.

The pursuit ended when a man, now 41, was struck by the police car as officers tried to bring Grainger to a stop. Officers stopped to give him first aid at the scene. GMP said his injuries have changed his life.

Grainger kept driving before abandoning the car on Wellington Street, where CCTV captured him and his three passengers running from it. He was arrested the next day, gave no comment in interview, and was found not to be insured to drive the car. The court ordered the Seat Leon to be destroyed.

One of the passengers, Teagan Clements, later gave police a false statement. She was given a 20-week prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, and 80 hours of unpaid work for making a false statement tendered in evidence.

Detective Sergeant Louise Warhurst, of GMP’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said Grainger had consciously chosen to drive after drinking, and that the injured man’s life had been fundamentally changed.

“This case serves as a stark reminder of the potentially life-changing consequences of drink-driving,” she said.

GMP’s release gives the prison term as “four years and five” without completing the figure. Rochdale Daily has asked the press office to confirm the full term and will update this report.

articles.title: Greater Manchester Police to host pop-up events to combat online scams in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: In a bid to protect shoppers from online fraud, Greater Manchester Police will hold pop-up events in Rochdale next week, providing essential advice and support.
articles.content_html:
In the lead-up to Christmas, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is organising pop-up fraud-prevention events in Rochdale to help shoppers avoid online scams.

The sessions will take place at Virgin Money on Yorkshire Street on Tuesday 10 November, and at Halifax on the same street on Wednesday 11 November, both from 10am to 1pm.

The events are being hosted by GMP’s Economic Crime Unit, which aims to educate the public about the various types of scams, from simple confidence tricks to sophisticated online fraud.

Attendees will have the opportunity to speak with police staff and volunteers about any concerns they may have regarding fraud and cyber crime.

GMP has emphasised the importance of staying informed about the latest scams and has provided tips to reduce the risk of becoming a victim.

These include never sharing passwords or personal details, regularly updating devices and apps, and ensuring that emails and attachments are only opened if they come from trusted sources.

These pop-up events are crucial as they provide direct access to expert advice and support for local residents, particularly during the busy shopping season. By attending, shoppers can better protect themselves from potential scams and ensure a safer festive period.

articles.title: Middleton pupils form giant star to celebrate Rhodes Green school's new name
articles.excerpt: The former Little Heaton primary school welcomed the Bishop of Middleton for a celebration of its new name, with classroom visits, worship and a tree planting.
articles.content_html:
Pupils at a Middleton primary school formed a giant star in their playground to celebrate its new name during a visit from the Bishop of Middleton.

Rhodes Green Church of England Primary School, on Boardman Lane in Rhodes, welcomed the Rt Revd Mark Davies on Thursday 5 November. Children, staff, parents and members of the community joined the celebrations, which included classroom visits, worship and the planting of a commemorative tree.

The school was previously known as Little Heaton CE Primary School. It changed its name in September to reflect its connection with the Rhodes community, where many of its pupils live. Rochdale Council's school directory also records the change.

The star reflected the school's Christian vision, “Shine as stars in the world”, with children lining up in the playground to form its outline for a photograph taken from above.

Headteacher Chloe Noon said: “Rhodes Green is about much more than a new name. It's about the school we're building together and making sure every child feels happy, safe and proud to belong here.”

She added: “We want our children to have big dreams, to believe in themselves and to know that they can achieve wonderful things. Seeing them come together today, and hearing Bishop Mark share that same message, has been really special for all of us.”

The head boy and head girl showed the Bishop around the school, taking him into classrooms to meet children from every year group before an assembly with families. Pupils and staff gave readings during the celebration.

Bishop Mark, who has known the school for more than 20 years, said: “Today has been absolutely amazing and such a tremendous joy and a great blessing. Today represents a new and exciting chapter. A name says so much and is so, so important.”

During a conversation with pupil leaders, he spoke about teachers and church leaders who had encouraged him and urged the children to believe in their own ambitions.

Cranmer Education Trust, which supplied the account of the visit, said the school joined the trust in 2024. Its chief executive Julie Hollis and chair of trustees Janet Gregory attended, alongside the Rev'd Jenni Beaumont from All Saints, Rhodes.

For families who know the school by its former name, Rhodes Green is the same Boardman Lane school. Its current information is available at https://www.rhodesgreen-primary.org/.

Do you have memories of Little Heaton, or a connection with Rhodes Green today? Share them in the comments.

articles.title: Middleton residents warned about scammers posing as council officials
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has issued a warning to residents in Middleton about scammers posing as council officials to gain entry into homes.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Middleton are being warned about scammers posing as council officials in an attempt to gain entry into their homes. This warning follows reports of several incidents in the area, prompting Rochdale Council to take action.

The council stated, "We have been made aware of bogus cold callers posing as council officers to gain entry into homes." They emphasised that all legitimate council staff carry identification and can produce it upon request.

Residents are advised to check for ID before allowing anyone into their homes.

If residents are unsure about a caller's identity or if they cannot produce an official badge, they are encouraged to refuse entry.

The council also reminded residents that services and appointments can only be booked and paid for in advance through their contact centre at 01706 647474.

Residents who have experienced similar visits are urged to report them to Greater Manchester Police, either online or by calling 101.

articles.title: Rochdale's pathology teams support millions of tests during National Pathology Week
articles.excerpt: As National Pathology Week is celebrated, Rochdale's pathology teams highlight their vital role in healthcare, processing over 10 million samples annually.
articles.content_html:
This week marks National Pathology Week, a time to recognise the essential work of pathology teams across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale.

These teams process more than 10 million samples and conduct over 35 million tests each year, playing a crucial role in patient care.

Pathology services are integral to approximately 95% of clinical pathways, providing the diagnostic information that clinicians rely on to diagnose illnesses, guide treatments, and monitor ongoing care. Despite their critical role, many patients may never meet the professionals working behind the scenes in pathology laboratories.

The Northern Care Alliance's pathology workforce includes nearly 700 staff members across various locations, including Rochdale, Oldham, Salford, and Bury. This diverse team comprises biomedical scientists, pathologists, clinical scientists, and other specialists who work together to ensure efficient and accurate testing.

Recent advancements in technology, such as the introduction of automated biopsy processing in Oldham, have improved workflow and increased capacity, allowing biomedical scientists to focus more on specialised diagnostic work.

As the healthcare landscape evolves, the importance of pathology services in supporting patient care continues to grow. The implementation of a new Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) has also transformed how laboratories manage samples and results, ensuring uninterrupted services for patients.

articles.title: Middleton council completes purchase of Warwick Mill to boost regeneration
articles.excerpt: The purchase of Warwick Mill and London House marks a significant step in Middleton's regeneration efforts, with plans for redevelopment underway.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration has taken a significant step forward with the Rochdale Borough Council completing the purchase of Warwick Mill from developer Kam Lei Fong.

The historic cotton mill, built in 1907, has been vacant for over a decade and has become a target for vandalism and urban explorers.

As part of the £3.3 million deal, the council also acquired the neighbouring London House, a 1960s office block that is set to be demolished.

The redevelopment of Warwick Mill is seen as a vital opportunity to restore an important historic building and create new homes for the local community.

Immediate actions include enhancing security at the site with a 24-hour presence from Rochdale firm Winterburns, which will also begin clearing debris, including over 1,000 tyres and overgrown vegetation.

The internal strip-out of both Warwick Mill and London House is expected to commence shortly, with demolition of London House planned for early next year.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed optimism about the redevelopment, stating it will not only improve the area but also provide much-needed housing.

articles.title: Boyes opens new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow
articles.excerpt: Discount chain Boyes will open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre, filling the gap left by Wilko's closure.
articles.content_html:
Discount chain Boyes is set to open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow, 6 November, at 9am. This new store will occupy the former Wilko site, which closed earlier this year, leaving a gap in the local retail landscape.

For the past few weeks, contractors and staff have been preparing the two-floor space to welcome customers. Boyes aims to provide a wide range of products, including everyday essentials, electrical items, DIY supplies, fashion, footwear, craft and hobby materials, homewares, and seasonal goods.

Local residents have expressed enthusiasm about the new store. Yvonne Marie Knott stated, "Boyes has everything you need in a store," while Sharon Dyson added, "Can’t wait, Middleton needs this."

Kathleen Hall also shared her excitement, saying, "Looking forward to it!"

The opening of Boyes is expected to bring a boost to the local economy and provide residents with a convenient shopping option. As the store prepares to welcome its first customers, it will help fill the retail void left by Wilko's closure.

articles.title: Resident escapes fire at Lonsdale Court sheltered housing in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A resident self-rescued from a fire at Lonsdale Court in Middleton, prompting a swift response from fire crews and support services.
articles.content_html:
A fire broke out in a second-floor flat at Lonsdale Court, a sheltered housing residence in Middleton, on the evening of 5 November. Fire crews from Chadderton, Blackley, and Heywood fire stations responded quickly to the incident, which was reported just before 7pm.

Eyewitnesses reported seeing multiple fire engines and police vehicles on Sedgley Street and Nelson Street as the emergency services arrived. One resident managed to escape the flat before firefighters arrived and was assessed at the scene by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS).

The fire service confirmed that all residents in the neighbouring flats were evacuated safely and are being supported by Rochdale Homes. Following the extinguishing of the fire, safety checks were conducted to ensure the building was secure for re-entry.

This incident underscores the importance of fire safety measures in residential settings, particularly for vulnerable populations such as the elderly. Residents are reminded to ensure their smoke alarms are functioning and to have an escape plan in place.

articles.title: Is there really a secret tunnel under Middleton between the Ring O’Bells and St Leonard’s?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape-passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to Middleton Parish Church; documentary and heritage records find the legend persistent but not proved.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape-passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to Middleton Parish Church; documentary and heritage records find the legend persistent but not proved.
articles.body:
Short answer: no verifiable evidence has been published that a continuous, built “secret tunnel” links the Ring O’Bells (the pub on St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. What you can find are a long-lived local tradition, repeated accounts of Civil War‑era finds beneath the pub’s cellar, and a striking absence of confirmation in the formal heritage record.

The essentials are straightforward and local. St Leonard’s (the parish church on New Lane) is a Grade I listed building with medieval and post‑medieval fabric; its National Heritage List entry (List Entry No. 1162332) records the church’s architectural and historic interest (the entry was first listed on 15 March 1957). The Ring O’Bells stands opposite the church in Middleton town centre and is widely described in local guides as among the older buildings around the square. Those two facts — an ancient church on a hilltop and an old inn across the way — are what make the tunnel story so durable. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

What the legend says. Local folklore collections and modern “haunt” guides tell a consistent tale: during the 1640s (the Civil War) a small band of Royalists used the pub cellars as a meeting place and, allegedly, an underground passage ran to the church so they could flee if Roundheads arrived. Later retellings add grisly details — bodies found under the cellar, weapons and buckles recovered, and a 20th‑century landlord struck by a flying stone in the cellar — items cited again and again by websites that collect local legends. Those sites also quote a dated newspaper reference (often given as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972). Folklore compendia are the source for these claims; they make the tradition both colourful and memorable, but they are not the same as an archaeological report or archive record. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

What the formal records say — and do not say. We looked for authoritative, primary confirmation: listed‑building records, conservation appraisals and the local conservation-area documentation, and the published local histories and antiquarian collections that are commonly used by historic‑environment professionals. Historic England’s list entry for St Leonard’s makes no mention of a connecting subterranean passage; nor does the Middleton Town Centre Conservation Area documentation held by Rochdale Council (the conservation‑area appraisal entry dates from 2009 in the council’s record). Those documents record built fabric, archaeological sensitivity and the townscape; they do not record a mapped, scheduled or otherwise recorded tunnel between the buildings. In short: the national register and local conservation material that would normally notice a known historic passage do not record one. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Is there any corroborated archaeological evidence? Several modern retellings repeat that Civil War‑period artefacts and human remains were recovered beneath the Ring O’Bells cellar. I found those claims repeatedly cited in folklore and local‑interest sources, and an antiquarian reference confirming the existence of local manors (Stannycliffe is recorded in older county sources), which explains why Royalists might have been present. However, I could not locate a publicly available archaeological report, museum accession record, or council excavation record that documents the recovery of dated musketry, pikes, buckles or skeletons from the pub which would meet the standards used by heritage professionals. Where the newspaper item from 1972 is quoted by later writers, I was unable to trace an on‑line copy of that original article in digitised newspaper archives during this check; later compendia appear to rely on that reporting. That leaves the finds — as reported in popular accounts — as plausible local memory or secondary reporting, but not as independently catalogued archaeological evidence. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/54/Chetham_miscellanies_%28IA_chethammiscellan19chet%29.pdf))

So what should a curious Middleton reader make of it? Treat the tunnel as a piece of local tradition that links real places and real Civil War histories, but not as an established archaeological fact. If someone wanted to move from story to proof the practical next steps are clear and formal: search the original local‑newspaper archives for the 1972 report; ask Rochdale Archives (and Lancashire record repositories) for any recorded finds from the Ring O’Bells; and, if physical evidence were produced, seek an archaeologist’s recording and a museum accession. Absent that, the story remains a well‑rooted and well‑repeated legend that helps explain why people still look at the gap between the church and the pub and imagine a passage underground.

Useful starting points for follow‑up (authoritative records consulted for this piece): Historic England’s National Heritage List entry for St Leonard’s Parish Church (the primary national record for the church’s significance) and Rochdale Council’s Middleton Town Centre conservation documentation. For the folklore and the repeated account of cellar finds, modern compendia of local ghost and legend material collect the variants of the story and the citations to the later newspaper coverage; they are useful to show how the tale is told, but they do not replace an excavation report or archive copy of the claimed press item. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has issued a warning to families after confirmed cases of measles were reported in the borough. The council highlighted that some of these cases have resulted in visits to Accident and Emergency departments, raising concerns about the potential spread of the virus.

Health officials are advising residents to be aware of the symptoms of measles, which include high fever, runny nose, cough, red and watery eyes, Koplik spots, and a rash that typically starts on the face and spreads across the body.

Measles can lead to serious health complications, particularly for vulnerable individuals such as infants and those with weakened immune systems.

The council has urged parents to ensure their children are vaccinated with the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine, which is usually administered at 12 and 18 months of age.

Those who have not yet received the vaccine are encouraged to contact their GP to arrange an appointment.

This warning serves as a crucial reminder for families in Rochdale about the importance of recognising measles symptoms and ensuring vaccinations are up to date. Vaccination can help prevent the spread of this highly contagious disease.

articles.excerpt: Roadworks on Moor Road in Littleborough will start on 5 November 2026, affecting local traffic for up to 21 days.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks on Moor Road in Littleborough will commence on 5 November 2026. The work is expected to last for a maximum of 21 days, concluding by 26 November 2026, or sooner if repairs are completed ahead of schedule.

The roadworks will result in a temporary closure of part of Moor Road, specifically from 104 metres north of the junction with Temple Kane to 10 metres further up the road. This closure will affect traffic flow, particularly for residents and commuters in the area.

Local roads including Calderbrook Road, Barnes Meadows, and Temple Lane may experience increased traffic as drivers seek alternative routes during the closure. Residents should plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

For more information on the roadworks and to view a map of the affected area, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale resident seeks planning permission for new garden wall and fencing
articles.excerpt: Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his home in Rochdale, which has raised concerns among local planners.
articles.content_html:
Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his property located at 1 Bates Close, Rochdale.

The application has sparked discussions among local planners regarding the impact of the new structure on the character of the surrounding area.

Planners have expressed concerns that the new fencing is out of character with the existing street scene, which typically features low-rise fencing and lacks hard boundary treatments.

This has led to a debate about how the new installation fits within the established aesthetic of Bates Close.

The planning committee is currently reviewing the application and considering the implications of the new wall and fencing on the neighbourhood's visual coherence.

The outcome of this review will determine whether the retrospective permission will be granted or if the structure will need to be modified or removed.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges residents face when making changes to their properties in ways that may not align with local planning guidelines. The decision will be significant for Mahoney and could set a precedent for similar applications in the area.

articles.title: The Baum Rabbit: the ghostly white hare that belonged to St Mary in the Baum
articles.excerpt: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.summary: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.body:
You can still stand outside St Mary in the Baum on St Mary’s Gate and see how easy it would have been, in the years before the town filled the fields, to imagine something uncanny stirring among the tombstones. The church on this site was founded as a chapel of ease in the 1740s; today’s building dates to 1909–11. Local history collections record that the graveyard and its approaches were long the stage for a phantom known in the Lancashire dialect as the Baum Rabbit (or Baum Rappit). That, at least, is what the nineteenth‑century parish histories and later compilers say.
